Industry News: How Will Robert Pattinson’s James Bond Dress?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (989 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that when Terence Young, the director of Dr.
  • Industry observers note that “Connery’s suits were considered relatively contemporary, because Anthony always had a very soft shoulder on his suits,” explains Elliot Mason, the director of business at Anthony Sinclair, which is no longer located on Savile Row, but still makes classic British suiting.
  • Opting to dress James Bond in a Savile Row suit might seem like a no-brainer in hindsight, but the decision—and the cut of the suits themselves—still resonates more than 60 years later.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that when Terence Young, the director of Dr. No, needed a suit for Sean Connery to wear for his debut as James Bond, he took him to see his personal Savile Row tailor, Anthony Sinclair.

Industry observers note that “Connery’s suits were considered relatively contemporary, because Anthony always had a very soft shoulder on his suits,” explains Elliot Mason, the director of business at Anthony Sinclair, which is no longer located on Savile Row, but still makes classic British suiting. “Anthony liked to nip in the waist, so it gave that real hourglass silhouette to the suit, which really is quite timeless. And as was the trend at the time, the Connery suits all had a relatively high rise, double-pleated with English forward pleats, and most of his trousers had Daks button-tab adjusters on the side.”.

Opting to dress James Bond in a Savile Row suit might seem like a no-brainer in hindsight, but the decision—and the cut of the suits themselves—still resonates more than 60 years later. Sinclair would make all of Connery’s suits during his nine-year run as James Bond, and his blend of classic British tailoring and of-the-moment influences would create a template for every Bond to come. With Robert Pattinson—a Dior ambassador and a guy with a reputation for adventurous style—chosen to take up the mantle in Bond 26, the question now becomes: what will he wear?

Tailor Anthony Sinclair fitting Sean Connery for one of the suits he wore in 1963’s From Russia With Love.

Sources indicate that ian Fleming, the author who created James Bond, spent a lot of time talking about what Agent 007 drank (Wolfschmidt Vodka) what he drove (Bentley convertibles, for the most part) and how he made his coffee (he was a dedicated pour-over guy), but, surprisingly, he never specified where the spy bought his clothes. As a result, for the last six decades, it’s been up to the directors and costume designers of the 25 previous films to create a new look for every successive Bond. In the Connery and Moore eras it was Savile Row suits. Timothy Dalton’s Bond wore Paul Smith. Brosnan was a bespoke Brioni guy, as was Daniel Craig, who also brought Tom Ford into the mix. At 6’1” to Craig’s 5’10”, with a leaner build, and a long track record of fashion-forward dressing, Pattinson has everything needed to reinvent Bond once again.

It has been revealed that “I’m pretty sure we’re going to see something quite different from Pattinson's Bond,” indicates Matt Spaiser, the tailoring obsessive behind BondSuits.com and the author of From Tailors with Love: An Evolution of Menswear Through the Bond Films. “Pattinson is a different kind of actor, and he’s going to wear something that moves differently. Plus, he’s 18 years younger than Daniel Craig.”.

Recent findings suggest that the actor playing Bond has a major influence on how he dresses—Daniel Craig, an adventurous dresser himself, was very hands-on with the wardrobe in his films—but Pattinson’s ongoing contract with Dior could also factor in. “Some of his Dior looks look somewhat like James Bond—he wears a great tuxedo—but I don’t think it’s going to tell us what he’s going to wear as James Bond,” Spaiser notes. “He’s worn suits from other brands in other roles—like in Tenet, he wasn’t wearing a Dior suit—so I don’t think he's necessarily obligated to be wearing Dior as James Bond.”.

Daniel Craig, seen here in 2019 with then-Prince Charles on the set of No Time to Die, mainly sported sharp Tom Ford suiting in his later Bond films.

Another notable factor that contributes to a fresh Bond’s look is what’s happening in fashion whenever the film eventually gets made. “One thing that we've seen throughout most of the Bond eras is that he dresses in suits that are fairly traditional, but there's always some nod to the era that they’re in,” indicates Spaiser. “Sometimes they lean a little more into fashion, like when Roger Moore was wearing flares. That was something that I think they couldn't avoid without making Bond look too old-fashioned at the time.”.

Industry observers note that tone also plays an key role, and historically has ping-ponged between serious (Connery, Dalton, Craig) and more campy (Moore, Brosnan), but with Denis Villeneuve, the auteur behind Sicario, Blade Runner: 2049, and Dune in the director’s chair, the smart money isn’t on hovercraft gondolas and punny Bond girl names. A darker, more atmospheric milieu could make for an interesting complement to Pattinson’s taste for high-fashion.

In a recent development, if Mason were dressing Pattinson for the role, he says, he’d take a lead from his clientele, many of whom, like Bond, are well-heeled Londoners with a taste for expensive sports cars and well mixed cocktails. “The majority of our customers are reasonably conservative, and when it comes to fit, they’re sensitive to current trends,” Mason notes. As such, he’d opt for longer jackets, both single- and double-breasted, that are fuller through the body, and straight-leg pleated trousers. “It’s not that very, very slim fit that we'd seen for so many years, but it still needs to be refined,” he says. “I don’t think it would be appropriate to put him in wide-leg or baggy trousers. I just don't think it’s right for Bond.”.

Robert Pattinson, the latest 007, has been the face of Dior’s menswear for over a decade.

Sources indicate that given the intense scrutiny on every relaunch of the Bond franchise, and the tendency of fans to get worked up online over perceived mishandling of a beloved character, Pattinson, Villeneuve, and the film’s yet-to-be-revealed costume designers have little room for error. Go too conservative and they’ll be accused of playing it safe; make Bond into a fashion guy, and they’ll incur the wrath of the traditionalists.

Sources indicate that “He needs to look current, but also timeless,” Spaiser says. “It’s a hard balance to find.”.

Bella Hadid’s Radical Vulnerability

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2724 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Harpersbazaar

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I first met Bella Hadid on a fashion shoot I was styling more than a decade ago.
  • A few days after the Victoria’s Secret show in October, Bella and I sat down to reflect on her career so far, forgiveness and success, turning 30, and where she goes from here.
  • Industry observers note that samira Nasr: This is a full-circle moment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I first met Bella Hadid on a fashion shoot I was styling more than a decade ago. We went on to shoot several stories together, including her first major American magazine cover. On one of those shoots, she arrived upset because she had just found out she didn’t get cast in the Victoria’s Secret show. I will never forget telling Bella that one day, Victoria’s Secret would be begging her to walk for them. Cut to today, and Bella is not only one of the most in-demand models, but she opened their most recent show. When I saw her hit the runway in a beaded floral bra and matching wings, I let out a scream because I knew what that moment meant to her.

A few days after the Victoria’s Secret show in October, Bella and I sat down to reflect on her career so far, forgiveness and success, turning 30, and where she goes from here. I have always felt connected to Bella because she, like me, is a heart-on-her-sleeve kind of gal. She is deeply vulnerable and human, and it’s what makes her one of the most compelling figures in fashion today.

Industry observers note that samira Nasr: This is a full-circle moment. On one of our first shoots together, you were really upset because you didn’t get the Victoria’s Secret show. And I said to you, “One day, they will be begging you to be in their show.” And I could tell you didn’t believe me. Your whole body shut down. And three days ago, you opened Victoria’s Secret. Holy shit.

Bella Hadid: I still don’t believe you, to be honest. I feel like people are just AI-ing me onto the runway. I think that it’s so crazy how time passes and you still have some kind of impostor syndrome. No matter how hard you work, there’s always another girl who is more deserving, more beautiful, and has worked so hard to be able to get that spot. Ten years ago, I remember that moment too, where I never thought I would get the show, but I think that God always has a plan, and I truly believe at that time I wasn’t ready. I don’t think I’ve been ready until this year, to be honest. In past years, I was going to my horse-show finals in the morning, flying straight to the Victoria’s Secret show that day, doing rehearsal right before, and then pulling what we call a Bella, and Belinda comes out, and we just act. But this year, I felt really strong.

Recent findings suggest that I have had to make a decision for myself to have boundaries with my own health. And I think it’s gotten me to this point now where I’m able to do the jobs that I do want to do with people that I love, that I can feel inspired by. And that’s truly what [working in] fashion is about: being around people you feel inspired by. Until you find that inspiration, it’s hard to go back into our industry. I think I needed a little bit of time just to be able to be like, “Let me just remember why I’m doing this again,” because I know I’m more than just a face.

Recent findings suggest that SN: We don’t really support a culture of care. I have always believed that boundaries are bridges.

In a recent development, BH: They really are. We know so many people who have been working for 30, 40, 50 years in this industry with zero boundaries. I’ve watched people over the years just get more depressed because they don’t know themselves and they don’t know who they are. And that’s how I was for 10 years, when I didn’t know what my favorite color was, what I liked to eat. I stopped listening to music. To not be able to know yourself in an industry that tells you how to be every single day is really hard.

SN: Going back to Victoria’s Secret, did you feel empowered, or was that your alter ego? What is her name again?

Sources indicate that BH: Belinda. You know what? Fortunately and unfortunately, I think it was Bella this year.

Sources indicate that SN: That’s great. I’m so happy for you.

In a recent development, BH: I made up my alter ego, Belinda, a long time ago to deal with the intensity of everything happening in my life. So she could deal with that, and I can deal with this, and we can do this together, which I’m realizing I should probably go to therapy about again. Belinda is the one that people are like, “Wow, this, that.”.

Recent findings suggest that I have POTS [postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome], and I have a lot of PMDD [premenstrual dysphoric disorder], endometriosis, plus my Lyme and things that affect my body very deeply. Right before I walked out on the runway for my opening look, I went to go stretch and my whole clavicle completely … I don’t even know what it was. My lungs almost collapsed, and I couldn’t breathe, and then it was like, “Five, four …” So my body goes through these different motions of feeling really good and then all of a sudden crashing on me at the worst moments. I need to realize maybe my body can’t handle all that I have going on. Because I know how to walk. One thing I can do is I can strut. But it’s a lot of pressure; we all have our own insecurities. Sometimes my body just can’t connect with my brain. My brain wants to do it, and my body is like, “No, we can’t do that today.” And I’m like, “Okay, great. So let’s figure out another way.” But I think people don’t realize how much I struggle with the fatigue and the body pain, and so I just try my best.

According to recent reports, SN: You’ve achieved so much in your 20s. You just turned 30. What are you looking forward to in your 30s?

According to recent reports, BH: It’s funny, today I woke up with—I wouldn’t say the word is anxiety, but this feeling of “Oh my gosh, my life is starting.” I want to get rid of what doesn’t bring me joy and bring in what does. I’ve tried to put myself in positions for work for a very long time that have made me feel out of body or like I don’t belong. Years ago, I was just grateful to get a job, and I would say yes to everything. I lacked boundaries then, but I do believe that that gave me the strength to be able to have the confidence in my own boundaries now. I’ve achieved pretty much all the goals that I wanted to when it comes to fashion as a model. And now I do want to go into other ventures to eventually get to peace and happiness and love within this universe that God has put me in.

In the next couple of years, it’s just about getting back to community, getting back to using my voice again. I got beaten down pretty heavy for a long time, which pushed me into this very big struggle with my physical and emotional health, which makes my brain turn off and makes me not be able to write or read. When you’re not around enough people that are like-minded, you feel really ostracized. That’s almost where I got to. Of course, I always want to speak from my heart, which I hope will never disrespect anybody, but still be able to have the confidence to speak my truth and hope that people will walk beside me along the way when it comes to that.

SN: Is there something you’re most proud of achieving?

According to recent reports, BH: Well, first and foremost, starting [my fragrance line] Orebella was something that I truly needed for my own creativity and to be able to build community. I am not a 50/50 person. I’m an all-in type of girl. Being able to move forward into my 30s, really focusing on building the things that I’ve started—Orebella was something that I pushed so hard for since 2018, and the fact that it’s really now coming to fruition makes me so proud.

According to recent reports, when I was 17, going to my first go-see with a stylist I will not name, I was basically told I was too substantial to wear Saint Laurent and needed to lose a couple of pounds. And that’s when I was just a baby coming out of high school. Twelve years later, now I’m the face of Saint Laurent. I’m the face of Prada, which is incredible and insane. Times have changed so much, and the people that have come into the industry to make it a better place for us as models are so crucial. Not that that comment ever impacted me. I went through enough struggles with my body before that, so by the time she said that, I was like, “Okay, girl, I’m actually coming out of something that I dealt with very heavily when it came to my body. And now I look at food in a different way, and I love my body, and that’s okay if you think that I don’t look the way that you think I should look.”.

I just would love for everyone to think about if every day they had to walk outside and be photographed, what that would feel like, because it’s an uncomfortable feeling for anybody. My face would change so much. I would be super puffy one day, and one day I would look yellow and emaciated, and people would think I was on drugs or doing this or that. And when anybody knows about, one, hormones, just as a woman in general, and two, about immune problems and how weight fluctuates—again, I just think that there needs to be more sensitivity in our industry.

SN: I’m curious if you’ve always been this person—so sensitive, empathetic—from a little girl.

Sources indicate that BH: I’ve always felt like my sensitivity and my openness were a disservice to myself because I felt like no one else was like me in those ways, so I shut it down. Now I realize that there is a generosity of thoughtfulness that is so much deeper than just buying somebody an expensive gift. I think sitting on the side of the street with somebody, even if you don’t have any money, is more crucial than just walking by without caring.

SN: You’re able to access compassion when a lot of people can’t, and that is a superpower. I want to talk about style because you mentioned your archive. I remember you once mentioned you collect Gaultier. Do you still collect?

Sources indicate that BH: I do collect. Behind me are bags to sell. But downstairs, I have my Gaultier dress that the atelier made. It was a Naomi Campbell dress that she had worn in one of their shows, and I was obsessed with it. I called their PR, and within a week and a half, because that dress was in a museum, I had it made and sent to Cannes, and that was that white-and-black dress that I wore on the carpet. And so, that’s here. My Coperni dress is here. I have a whole section for Virgil [Abloh].

SN: The last time I saw Virgil was with you, actually.

BH: I don’t think I’ve done a real, full Fashion Month since he passed away. And Vivienne [Westwood] and Karl [Lagerfeld] passed, and I felt like all of my idols were leaving, and it felt really scary. I have all the art Virgil gave me, his letter he wrote me, his bags, his shoes he made me. And then I have my Prada area, my Cavalli area, my Bob Mackies that I’ve been collecting over the years.

BH: Hopefully for a future wedding. There are just some dresses you can’t find again. And Bob did it best.

Sources indicate that SN: He’s an American icon. I wanted to talk to you about Cannes. You’re such a queen of Cannes now, and I look forward to seeing you there. Is it fun?

According to recent reports, BH: This past year was fun. I felt grounded. To do the red carpet and feel, in those moments, sober and happy and healthy and strong, and go to sleep not having anxiety about going out or how I’m going to look the next day, and just being with loved ones. It did really well for me this year.

Cannes has always held a very special place in my heart. It begins long before I arrive. Working closely with designers on custom gowns, exchanging references, and watching those first sketches come to life is such a beautiful part of the experience.

This year, being there to support Marie-Clémentine Dusabejambo’s Ben’Imana, the first Rwandan film in the official selection, was especially meaningful. It explores memory and reconciliation after the genocide against the Tutsi through women whose lives carry its legacy. That’s what I love about cinema: It brings us closer and gives stories too rarely heard the attention they deserve. You can enter a theater knowing nothing of someone’s world and leave carrying a little of it with you.

Industry observers note that SN: I look at you and how hard you’ve worked for so long, from our first job together. To me, it feels like you’ve achieved so much. But what does success look like for you? Do you feel you’ve achieved it?

Sources indicate that BH: I talked to my business manager yesterday, so that made me feel a little bit more successful. But when you don’t think about the money part of it, I think success truly comes from peace within. At the end of the day, I really don’t need much. That’s why I do give back so much, because a lot of the money that I do make, I don’t feel deserving of. There are so many people in the world, whether it’s doctors or teachers, that I think deserve my pay rate a lot more than I do.

Industry observers note that from an external space, success is about how known you are, how much you make, how many times you can be on TV, how many covers you’re on, how many fashion demonstrates you do. And that is really crucial in our industry, especially when you’re building. But for me, I am different. Success, for me, can be living in peace, in a small town, with a man that I love, with my child, having my animals. I’ve always wanted to start a farm-to-table bakery, with flowers, and everything comes from the community. I want to do things that are fulfilling for me in my soul: having a greenhouse that I can garden in, having my glassblowing and ceramic studio, and having lots of children and being a mother. It wasn’t a dream that I’ve always had, but it’s something that now is so intense for me. My intuition is screaming so loudly at me about it.

I think knowing there is a reason behind everything is so important. My sister and I donated a million dollars to Palestine last year [the donation was split between HEAL Palestine, Palestine Children’s Relief Fund, World Central Kitchen, and United Nations Relief and Works Agency], which we could have never been able to do without the success that we’ve had.

Sources indicate that god gave me the platform to be able to speak about the things that I hold dearly to me. And when it comes to Palestine or Sudan or Congo or Rwanda or places that mean so much to not only myself but the people around me—to give people a voice in any capacity, that’s success for me as well. To make my family wide and far proud, or to see themselves in me, it gives me strength.

This story appears in the Winter concern of Harper’s Bazaar.

What’s a Vintage Car Rally Really Like? Inside the Louis Vuitton Dolomites Classic Run.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In vintage rally driving, there are generally two types of competitor.
  • Gianandrea Redaelli, a car nut whose family has long roots in the Italian printing business, is firmly in the “road book” camp.
  • Venice might not seem the most logical starting line for a car rally given the proverbial wetness of the streets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In vintage rally driving, there are generally two types of competitor. Both share a passion for keeping priceless and nearly century-old vehicles in use on the open road rather than displaying them under glass. But some see the drive itself as challenge enough, while stalwarts adhere to what’s called the road book. This is a hundred or so pages of complex navigational directions that the copilot uses to navigate instead of a map, maintaining a constant flow of instructions to the driver. It is this book and how closely you follow it that decides the eventual winner.

Gianandrea Redaelli, a car nut whose family has long roots in the Italian printing business, is firmly in the “road book” camp. In early September, I climbed into the copilot seat of his 1939 Aston Martin C-Type Speed Model Roadster Bertelli—just one of two ever built, with an experimental aerodynamic body that earned it the nickname “the Flying Pea”—and stayed there as he drove six hundred kilometers of “left at the traffic lights, right at the cow” for the Louis Vuitton Dolomites Classic Run. The rally started in Venice and ended, after a scenic but challenging detour high into the Dolomite mountains, at Monza, the home of Italian Formula 1, just in time for practice day of the Grand Prix.

Venice might not seem the most logical starting line for a car rally given the proverbial wetness of the streets. But the city was chosen this year because it was also the end point of the last LV rally of its kind: the La Serenissima Run from Monte Carlo to Venice in 2012. Gianandrea won that one as copilot, with his father, Giuseppe, at the wheel. The pair also won the one before it—the Boheme across Hungary, the Czech Republic, and Austria—in 2006. This time, however, the pressure was on me too.

I have been a copilot before, and I can tell you it’s no picnic. Rally racing in vintage cars is less about speed and more about timing. It’s an exercise that requires pinpoint accuracy at the time-stamp points in the overall course and, most critically, in the regularities. These are fiendishly short time-over-distance sections in which crossing the line just a few hundredths of a second late—or early—earns strict penalties. Sensibly, the day before the race began, Gianandrea took me out in the Aston in the Veneto countryside to practice, especially those critical regularities.

I could have opted for an easy life. The rally allowed competing cars, dating from 1931 to 1969, to use the road book or follow the course using a map in a dedicated phone app. But where’s the fun in that?

“If you join a competition, you follow the regulations and strive to do your best,” Gianandrea states. “As an Italian, if you paint numbers on the door of my car, I will want to win.”.

According to recent reports, every car in a rally like this comes with its own idiosyncrasies. On flat ground, someone driving a souped-up 2026 sports car would find these tests difficult to nail. In the reality of race conditions, the regularities often involve steep climbs or descents and unexpected corners, alling for an expert hand at the wheel—and foot on the gas pedal. The tendency of some car doors to swing open at hard bends (ours has the “suicide” doors with hinges on the back instead of the front, beloved by early carmakers) only adds to the excitement. The purpose of driver and copilot is to battle and overcome all the mechanical and computational challenges—and get our ride to the finish line bang on time.

Recent findings suggest that louis Vuitton has been involved in these glamorous and exacting vintage rallies since 1993. The Dolomites Run represents an enthusiastic return to the genre after a fourteen-year gap and, perhaps tellingly, the company’s global sponsorship (since 2025) of Formula 1. Unconfirmed rumors circulated in the field that the choice of ending the rally at a Grand Prix could well be repeated—and soon—in other countries in the future.

According to recent reports, it’s easy, after all, to see why a fusion of style and cars with six- and seven-figure price tags might appeal to Louis Vuitton and competitors alike. Not surprisingly, at every coffee and lunch stop, the LV effect sprinkled the race with an added sense of luxury. In between, our snaking caravan carried the glamour of a century of motoring along with it. At every hairpin you got a glimpse of a gull-wing Mercedes, a 1931 Bugatti two-seater (my personal fave), and a shimmering behemoth of a Bentley in quick succession. These cars would turn heads anywhere. But in Italy, arguably the home of the sports car, they brought smiles, applause, and gasps in even the tiniest village that passed by in our slipstream. I swear I even saw a nun with a glint in her eye at one set of traffic lights.

According to recent reports, navigating, I was promptly learning, is not so much about providing a constant babble of information as it is knowing how to give clear and simple instructions—and only when strictly needed. As the finish neared in Monza at the end of two long days on the road, I was able to give Gianandrea the most helpful instruction of all: “Nothing for 15 kilometers.”.

“That,” he very kindly replied, “is the mark of a pro.”.

Even after the engines cooled, we were still clueless about how well we’d done overall. That changed at the final event, a dinner inside the Sforzesco Castle in Milan. Gianandrea stepped up, beaming, as winner of the race, and for the first time as driver. I stood somewhat sheepishly behind him as copilot as he received the trophy from Pietro Beccari, CEO of both Louis Vuitton and Louis Vuitton Fashion Group. It was an impressive swirl of Murano glass created by Venini, housed in its own equally impressive traveling case, made (naturellement) at Louis Vuitton’s atelier in Asnières.

Gianandrea has promised me visiting rights.

Welcome to In Good Company, where we ring in the festive season with fashion-insider entertaining tips, expert etiquette advice, and the perfect editor-approved hostess gifts.

According to recent reports, “I wanted to live in a white cube, only to end up building a whole business around the interiors I grew up in,” says Martina Mondadori, a Milanese tastemaker and the co-founder and editor in chief of Cabana. Mondadori’s home, dubbed Casa Cabana, is a true expression of that sensibility: a richly layered apartment designed by Renzo Mongiardino, the master of theatrical interiors and modern baroque, who was a close friend of her mother, its original owner.

Sources indicate that mondadori carried that more-is-more, layered sensibility into both Cabana, her lifestyle magazine turned home brand, and the way she entertains. Her Milan Fashion Week luncheons, hosted at her family home, have become a social fixture for a stalwart collective of designers, artists, and friends of the brand—from ELLE editor-in-chief Nina Garcia and La DoubleJ designer J.J. Martin to architects Roberto Peregalli and Laura Sartori Rimini—who gather over fresh pasta, delicious antipasto, and mouthwatering desserts beneath a canopy of color and pattern.

Industry observers note that “Ambiance is not only décor; it’s how you entertain, how you bring your friends and family together, how you gather them around the table—the food, the scent, the music,” she indicates, noting that it can take more than two years for a house to truly feel like home. “Mongiardino was so good at [creating ambiance] because he knew how to make coziness happen.”.

According to recent reports, for Mondadori, a beautiful table or a beautifully decorated space is only the beginning. She notes that any worthwhile gathering requires a “surgical” guest list layered with people from a “mishmash of different worlds,” plus tactile, personal touches like handmade place cards (often designed by her daughter, Cosima) and a guest book to capture the evening—her favorite hostess touch. Years later, its pages become a record of the people who have gathered around her table.

In a recent development, you have to be surgical about it. Whatever the size of the party, you need at least one or two great conversation starters—people who can bring others together and spark interesting connections. I also love mixing crowds from different industries, which a city like Milan, Newly introduced York, or London allows. When I was growing up in Milan in the ’80s, the fashion crowd and old industrial Milan were separate. Now there’s a much bigger creative industry, along with interesting visitors from abroad. I love bringing those people together.

Sources indicate that we usually spend Christmas Eve and Christmas Day in the mountains with our extended family. We play board games, sit around the table, and exchange gifts—it’s all about creating a happy atmosphere. I ask my daughter to craft the place cards. When we moved here, she was 4, and so the first ones were all kind of scrabbled and very sweet. And now she’s very artistic, so they’re getting more creative and neat.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The day after Valentine’s Day last year, my friend Tran casually texted me, asking, “You get into this guy?” with a Spotify link to an album called Heavy Metal by someone called Cameron Winter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Cambridge Dictionary recently declared that its selection for Word of the Year is human. Human as an adjective that denotes that something was not made by computers or A.I. (Last year’s word was parasocial.) The editor at Cambridge told the Times that they found phrases like “human governance,” “human written,” and “human need” come up often in their research.

According to recent reports, I think about this while I’m at the movie theater watching Paul Thomas Anderson’s latest film, Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall, which documents the 23-year-old’s performance at the legendary venue. It is the film’s release date, and all of the showings are sold out, but since I’ve come alone, I am able to find the perfect seat. Winter’s face is large on the screen, and it’s almost expressionless except for his eyebrows, barely peeking out from underneath what can truly only be called a mop of hair, which curves this way and that way as the only proof of the emotional energy he is exerting. Otherwise, he seems to simply open his mouth and the words come out, devastating and romantic, because what else would they do? What else would he do but this? For an hour and a half, we all sit here enthralled by a single man and a piano. Then I think about how my most recent moviegoing experiences required staring at people talking, or thinking, or simply staring at a very close range. (I’d just seen You Can See Everything a few weeks before.) We come to the movies to see humans was my brain-rot thought, in the style of Nicole Kidman’s famous AMC commercial. (Brain rot was Oxford’s 2024 Word of the Year.).

I think back to when it all began. The day after Valentine’s Day last year, my friend Tran casually texted me, asking, “You get into this guy?” with a Spotify link to an album called Heavy Metal by someone called Cameron Winter. I couldn’t tell what it would sound like just by looking at the cover, which was a close-up of his face, criss-crossed by silver chains, but what I soon found were songs dominated by a deep baritone voice and a sweet, jangly guitar or a kind of hazily sensual piano. Who was this guy? Well, it turned out he was the lead singer of this band called Geese—not to be confused with Goose—which he’d started when he was a teen with his high school friends. He’d made this album (jokingly rumored to have been recorded in Guitar Centers, from which he was now banned) and released it without any fanfare that previous December, against the advice of people who knew him and thought the record was too strange or would somehow interfere with the planned Geese release in the new year. (That album, Getting Killed, was released in September 2025 and turned the band from little-known Brooklyn musicians into both “saviors of rock & roll” and “music label psy-ops,” topping off numerous best-of lists and garnering multiple Grammy nominations.) But none of that had happened yet.

As I sat in the movie theater, I wondered how many of us in the audience had also been at the performance. What were we looking for in a recording of something we had experienced firsthand? That night, Winter emerged on stage and sat at the piano, his back turned to us. We watched his head sink beneath his shoulders as if he was searching for something deeper inside the instrument, or maybe he was becoming one with it. We had no choice but to completely give ourselves to the music. But Anderson’s camera was nimble and dug itself in other places: a peephole on the stage that looked out to Winter in the foreground and the ocean of people behind him, indeed turning the whole affair into a kind of landscape, swooping in from the audience to Winter at the piano like a detective looking for the culprit of an unnamed crime, or training his lens on the oversize shadow cast by Winter over the audience sitting stage left. I think, “Oh, this is like a musical Rashomon.”.

During “Drinking Age,” as he sings, “Today, I met who I’m gonna be / from now on / and he’s a piece of shit,” the screen goes dark blue, with only his faint silhouette visible, the weight of his words carrying a brief silence so that you sit there in the emotion. Other times, we experience through Anderson’s POV, seeing the ushers open the backstage doors so that he can step onstage, deftly twirling the camera around Winter’s body. This time he is singing “$0.” It’s perhaps the best song on the album (or at least according to this writer), where he sings with wild abandon, “God is real / God is real / I’m not kidding, God is actually real I’m not kidding this time / I think God is actually for real …” Anderson trains his camera on one of the dramatic light fixtures at the concert hall, a round disc that resembles the sun, then he pans to the audience, then to Winter, small on stage, confessing his small miracle. Afterward, as if exhausted, he delicately plays a simple riff on the piano, while there’s a close-up of his face on screen with heavenly rays of light reflected on his face. I believed him when I first heard it on the album, and I believed him twice more as I heard him sing it live.

According to recent reports, winter stands up; the show is over. The lights come up, and the crowd rises to its feet. I can’t remember now if there was an encore, though I do remember we stood there applauding for a very long time, emotionally drained but joyful that we’d been witnesses. On the screen, the credits roll over images of the crowd, and the two teen girls sitting to my right have spotted themselves in the audience, elated. Winter comes back out for two more songs.

The movie ends. “Cameron Winter. Live at Carnegie Hall. Dead at 23,” flashes on the screen. Inside the movie theater, the people applaud. I’m still thinking of Winter singing of “com[ing] down to see / my private ceremonies / All on the floor of this room,” and I think, yes, we’re all here in ceremony—or are we in communion?—with one another. The human need for human connection, for human revelations.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

In a recent development, we lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

It has been revealed that across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Welcome to In Good Organization, where we ring in the festive season with fashion-insider entertaining tips, expert etiquette advice, and the perfect editor-approved hostess gifts.

Madame Isabelle d’Ornano’s early gatherings at her family’s Loire Valley estate were dressy affairs. Over time, the Sisley Paris matriarch—whose plant-based approach helped redefine the beauty industry—let the formality fall away. Grand dinners became generous buffets of moussaka, poached eggs over lentil salad, and even “pizza à la d’Ornano.” The mood is more relaxed now, but the thoughtfulness remains—a sensibility she shares in her new book, Imagine: Words & Cushions, and has passed on to her children, including Countess Christine d’Ornano.

“I started to embroider the words ‘love’ and ‘peace.’ People wanted to buy my cushions. I said no,” she remembers with a laugh. “My cushions are much, much too precious.”.

That sense of personal attachment runs through d’Ornano’s home, too. At 89, she lives on Paris’s Left Bank in a maximalist duplex layered with Henri Cartier-Bresson photos and objects by Jean-François Fourtou. (She shared the home with her late husband, Hubert d’Ornano, with whom she co-founded Sisley.) It’s also where she welcomes family for the holidays, a tradition that reflects her easy approach to entertaining: She likes a mélange of guests, from the glamorous to those for whom an invitation “feels like a treat.”.

Sources indicate that her family knows just how much the cushions mean to her—and still hopes to get one. “My daughter-in-law and my granddaughter say, ‘If you give me one present, give me a cushion,’” she says. “Because I’m quite stingy with my cushions.”.

In a recent development, if it’s a big party, the more glamorous people you have, the better. But you also need people who really like you, and some for whom it’s a treat to be there. It’s a mixture.

Recent findings suggest that I would not be able to live in a home that has been created and decorated by an architect, because I like having my mess and books around. You must not have too many rules.

Christmas is a wonderful tradition in our home. I made a cushion embroidered with “Noël”—it’s such a lovely word in French. Our family has come together every Christmas since I got married. And of course, we love presents, too.

Bella Hadid may be the face of Saint Laurent and Prada, and she may own every high-profile runway she’s on, but her long-term life goal doesn’t involve spotlights or mega fame. In her new cover story for Harper’s Bazaar, the supermodel opens up like never before about what she sees for her future.

Industry observers note that “From an external space, success is about how known you are, how much you make, how many times you can be on TV, how many covers you’re on, how many fashion highlights you do. And that is really important in our industry, especially when you’re building,” she notes. “But for me, I am different.”.

While she feels endlessly lucky for her place in the fashion industry, and admits that having opened the Victoria’s Secret fashion show last month was a dream come true, she yearns for an easy life surrounded by family and nature.

“Success, for me, can be living in peace, in a small town, with a man that I love, with my child, having my animals,” Hadid says.

A cowgirl at heart, the Orebella founder has down-to-earth goals that do not necessarily involve modeling, but do involve having a small local business, leaning into hobbies that bring her peace, and becoming a wife and mother.

Sources indicate that “I’ve always wanted to start a farm-to-table bakery, with flowers, and everything comes from the community. I want to do things that are fulfilling for me in my soul: having a greenhouse that I can garden in, having my glassblowing and ceramic studio, and having lots of children and being a mother,” she states. “It wasn’t a dream that I’ve always had, but it’s something that now is so intense for me. My intuition is screaming so loudly at me about it.”.

Welcome to In Good Company, where we ring in the festive season with fashion-insider entertaining tips, expert etiquette advice, and the perfect editor-approved hostess gifts.

In a recent development, despite creating elaborate floral arrangements for the crème de la crème of luxury fashion, Mark Colle prefers a humbler bouquet to gift. “If I give flowers to someone, I buy them at the gas station,” he says plainly. “They have a trashy charm to them that I appreciate.”.

It has been revealed that that irreverent sensibility sits at the heart of the Belgian florist’s métier: Flowers should shock and delight—and sometimes make you squirm. “I want people to be surprised most of all, which, with social media and Instagram, is becoming more difficult,” he claims. Take his collaboration with Glenn Martens for Maison Margiela’s spring/summer 2027 runway show. It was the punkier answer to Colle’s arrangements for Raf Simons’s Dior couture debut in 2012, when he transformed the rooms of a Paris hôtel particulier with a million blooms.

For Margiela, he lined seven rooms with flowers at different stages of decay, with the blooms left to show their age. “I start with color, [that] is always the most notable to me,” he notes. “Dior, for example. You have red, pink, and gray. But it’s a very specific red and a very specific pink. It’s maybe not so much about flower, but more about the color the flower has.”.

Sources indicate that it takes a sure hand to make flowers feel at home in a space—whether that’s a runway, a grand gala, or your dining room table—something Colle knows well. For arrangements, he looks to flowers with personality, like goldenrod, a bright, textural accent, or dahlias, whose many different forms can set very different moods. Colle’s anything-goes floral work has caught the attention of a who’s who of fashion heavyweights, from Saint Laurent and Chloé to Louis Vuitton and Prada, whose co-creative director Raf Simons first crossed paths with him while shopping for plants at his Antwerp shop, Baltimore Bloemen.

Here, Colle talks about choosing flowers, creating a mood, and finding inspiration in the unexpected.

Sources indicate that dahlias. They come in so many different shapes and colors. You can use them for something that resembles a medieval painting, but you could also use them for something that needs to look very futuristic, because there are certain typesthat have super-colorful spikes. But for me, it can be any flower, really. There is nothing that I consider ugly or unusable. It depends on the context or how you use it.

Nobody ever gives me flowers. But if I give flowers to somebody, I honestly buy them at the gas station, because they have a trashy charm to them that I really appreciate. And also, it’s not what people expect to receive from me flower-wise.

Goldenrod, which over here is associated with something you would find in a gas station bouquet, so to speak, because it has no presence at all. But for me, that makes it interesting that you can use this common flower that people even almost look down upon into something very chic. That’s sometimes a nice challenge for me.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, squash and sausage are a heroic autumnal pairing, especially in a weeknight-friendly pasta. Butternut is the easiest squash to source—not to mention easily found peeled and chopped (a blessing for those with more timid knife skills). But other winter squash like acorn or red kuri can stand in as desired. Whichever squash you select, a sharp, heavy chef’s knife is best for breaking down the chunky veg. But to make your life easier, microwave the squash for 1 to 2 minutes. It will slightly soften, making it simpler—and safer—to slice through.

Rigatoni’s ribbed surface and large holes help chunky squash sauce cling and bites of seared sausage and date wedge—opting for a nutty whole wheat variety will only add to this meal’s autumnal earthiness.

More cozy pastas this way: Balsamic Mushroom and Sausage Pasta; Creamy Red Curry Pasta; and Baked Feta Pasta With Green Sauce.

It has been revealed that cook 1 medium butternut squash (1½–2 lb.), peeled, halved, seeds removed, cut into 1" pieces (about 6 cups), in a large pot of boiling salted water until very tender, 12–14 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer squash to a medium bowl. Reduce heat to low, cover pot, and leave on burner to keep warm.

According to recent reports, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium Dutch oven over medium-high. Add 1 lb. hot or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and break up into small pieces with a wooden spoon. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, about 3 minutes. Continue to cook, stirring occasionally, until browned all over and just cooked through, 3–4 minutes more. Transfer to a plate with a slotted spoon.

According to recent reports, reduce heat to medium-low. Cook 3½ oz. Medjool dates (about 6), pitted, sliced lengthwise ¾" thick, in same pan, turning halfway though, until deeply browned, 3–4 minutes. Transfer to plate with sausage; season with salt.

In a recent development, add remaining 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil to pan. Add 6 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and reserved squash. Cook, scraping up browned bits and smashing squash with spoon to break up, until lightly browned and broken up into a chunky paste (pieces do not need to be even), about 5 minutes.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, return cooking liquid in reserved pot to a boil over high heat. Cook 12 oz. short tube pasta (such as rigatoni) until very al dente, about 3 minutes less than package directions (it will finish cooking in sauce). Drain, reserving 3 cups pasta cooking liquid.

It has been revealed that add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid to squash and break up squash with spoon until a saucy consistency. Add pasta, another 1 cup pasta cooking liquid, and reserved sausage and dates. Increase heat to medium-high; cook, adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is al dente and coated in sauce, 2–3 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. sherry vinegar or balsamic vinegar. Taste pasta and add more vinegar, salt and/or pepper if needed.

Can 4 Minutes of Exercise a Day Really Improve Your Fitness?

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Committing to any level of exercise isn’t easy, even whether you’re a gym regular.
  • Time may not matter as much as you think.
  • “The best four-minute workout is one that challenges your body appropriately.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Committing to any level of exercise isn’t easy, even whether you’re a gym regular. But a recent Penn State College of Medicine study may be music to the ears of anyone looking to get active with minimal effort—especially older adults. The findings suggest that four minutes a day of strength training helped improve leg strength and balance in adults 65 and older. The benefits are significant for study participants, but whether the results translate to younger folks is up for debate. Dr. Harry Pino, director of human performance and exercise physiology at Yunara, unpacks if four minutes of exercise can help make gains or if it’s all too good to be true.

Time may not matter as much as you think. But before diving into the details of your workout, Pino suggests figuring out your goals and assessing your current fitness level. If you’re unsure which exercises work best for your end results, Pino offers this breakdown:.

“The best four-minute workout is one that challenges your body appropriately. Intensity matters, but consistency and progressive improvement are what drive long-term results,” Pino tells ELLE.

Recent findings suggest that it may seem insignificant and the warm-up may take longer than the exercises themselves, but Pino states four minutes can make a measurable difference, especially for someone who’s been sedentary. “Research reveals that brief daily strength workouts can improve balance, leg strength, and mobility in older adults. These improvements directly support physical function and independence as we age.”.

It has been revealed that the good news is yes, absolutely. According to Pino, exercise benefits are cumulative, and even brief sessions can stimulate positive adaptations when performed consistently. “Four minutes won’t replace a comprehensive fitness routine, but it’s an excellent starting point. Small, sustainable habits often produce the greatest long-term impact,” he says.

It has been revealed that focus on exercises that match your goals and fitness level. Pino’s recommendation is to start with a simple routine that might include 30 seconds each of squats, push-ups, step-ups, and resistance band rows, alternating with 30 seconds of recovery. “Prioritize proper form and gradually increase the challenge as your fitness improves,” he specifies.

Sources indicate that even a short workout benefits from a warm-up, particularly at higher intensities. Start with gentle movement to prepare your muscles and joints. Afterward, prioritize hydration, adequate nutrition, and quality sleep. Pino notes that exercise provides the stimulus, but recovery allows the body to adapt.

Sources indicate that there is no one-size-fits-all workout routine, no matter your body type or how active you are. “Fitness level, strength, and mobility are much more important than body shape when designing a workout. Beginners may benefit from modified movements, while more experienced individuals can increase resistance or intensity. The goal is to challenge the body safely and progressively," notes Pino.

According to recent reports, the Penn State study only studied an older set of adults, primarily to understand how to prevent falls and balance concerns that can come with age. While Pino explained that these findings can have a positive impact for anyone looking to get active, he agrees that short workouts can be especially valuable for older adults. “They’re accessible and easier to maintain consistently. Even a few minutes of daily strength training can improve balance, mobility, and functional strength. These improvements are critical for preserving independence and quality of life as we age,” Pino says.

Creamy Miso Mushroom Pasta

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mushroom fans: Bookmark this recipe immediately.
  • In a recent development, A few helpful notes for pasta success: (1) While any pasta will work, egg-based noodles, like the fettuccine I recommend here, are the best complement to the sauce.
  • Find more fall favorite meals here: Weeknight Pumpkin Chili; Cream-ish of Mushroom Soup; Mushrooms au Poivre.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mushroom fans: Bookmark this recipe immediately. It will give you everything you want when you crave a creamy mushroom pasta as soon as the crisp fall air sets in. The hardworking trio of miso, Parmesan, and touch of soy sauce delivers an umami bomb of flavor that doesn’t overwhelm, but magnifies, the best of earthy mushrooms. Coupled with luscious noodles enrobed in a creamy (but not heavy) sauce, what’s not to love?

In a recent development, A few helpful notes for pasta success: (1) While any pasta will work, egg-based noodles, like the fettuccine I recommend here, are the best complement to the sauce. The nests (Rummo and De Cecco are great accessible brands) cook far faster than standard straight pasta, almost as fast as fresh. (2) Don’t be afraid to season your mushrooms! Yes, I know this goes against all that we’ve learned about salting them too early in the cooking process, but just a bit of salt will get them going and releasing their water faster for eventual crisp-browned edges. Don’t be alarmed if you see a pool of water at the start of the mushroom cooking—that’s to be expected and just keep going until it evaporates. (3) Don’t forget to reserve plenty of pasta cooking liquid, which is critical to the eventual sauce’s success. I prefer transferring the al dente noodles from the pasta pot to the skillet, letting any residual water come with it (and to ensure you don’t accidentally drain away that liquid gold).

Find more fall favorite meals here: Weeknight Pumpkin Chili; Cream-ish of Mushroom Soup; Mushrooms au Poivre.

Cook 12 oz. egg-based pasta (such as fettuccine nests) in a large pot of boiling salted water, stirring occasionally, until al dente, about 1 minute less than package directions.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet over high. Add 1 lb. crimini or mixed mushrooms (such as button, maitake, oyster, and/or shiitake), sliced ¼" thick or torn into bite-size pieces, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and toss to coat evenly. Spread out into an even layer and cook, undisturbed, until mushrooms are starting to release their liquid, 2–3 minutes (do not be alarmed; there will be a lot). Continue to cook, tossing occasionally, until moisture is almost completely evaporated and edges of mushrooms are starting to brown, 6–8 minutes.

Recent findings suggest that reduce heat to medium-high; add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, tossing often, until garlic is fragrant and golden, 1–2 minutes. Pour in ¾ cup dry white wine, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan with a sturdy spatula or flat-edged wooden spoon, and cook until wine is mostly evaporated (you should have about 1 Tbsp. liquid left in pan), about 4 minutes. Reduce heat to medium-low. Add 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and 2 Tbsp. white miso and stir until melted and combined. Slowly pour in ½ cup heavy cream, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan; simmer until thickened slightly, 2–3 minutes. Add 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce; season with freshly ground pepper. Taste and add more salt if needed.

It has been revealed that using tongs, transfer pasta to mushroom mixture and add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Increase heat to medium and bring to a simmer. Cook, tossing constantly and adding ½–1 cup more pasta cooking liquid to reach desired sauce consistency if needed, until pasta is al dente and liquid has thickened slightly, about 3 minutes.

Remove pan from heat. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup) to pasta and toss to combine. Season generously with more pepper; taste and season with more salt if needed.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan and pepper.

This story contains spoilers for The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, the book and the film.

Ahead of the release of The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, author Suzanne Collins penned a letter sharing how grateful she was to have creatives on the production team who aspire to remain true to her source material.

“Sometimes you see a book as merely a springboard, but [producer Nina Jacobson] was committed to developing a faithful version of the series and has followed through by being an exceptional ambassador for the franchise,” Collins stated. Of Francis Lawrence, the film’s director, she added that he “helmed an extraordinary film which maintains the book’s narrative and themes.”.

Industry observers note that but as every fan knows, making a direct recreation of a book for the big screen is a challenging task that often leaves material on the cutting room floor. Sunrise on the Reaping ultimately overcomes those challenges for a faithful adaptation, but there are some notable discrepancies. Read on to find out what the movie did differently.

With the help of his District 3 ally, Ampert, Haymitch is able to successfully break into Sub-A and plant his explosive with no problems. The plan actually works so well that book Haymitch wonders if he messed up the instructions for planting the bomb.

Industry observers note that in the movie, this moment has a bit more added drama. As soon as he plants the explosive, four Peacekeepers spot Haymitch and attempt to capture him. Haymitch successfully escapes, blows up Sub-A, and temporarily shuts down the arena—but not without President Snow promptly receiving word of his actions over a phone call. He orders a dangerous volcano to enter the arena, no matter how many tributes it kills.

Sources indicate that in the movie, President Snow is out for blood after finding out what Haymitch did. He immediately investigates who could have instigated the plan and has Plutarch Heavensbee—who aided Haymitch in the plot—beaten and questioned by Peacekeepers.

Snow ultimately apologizes to Plutarch in the movie after learning that Beetee confessed to devising the entire plot, and looks on having Haymitch swiftly killed in the arena until Plutarch suggests an alternative. Instead of killing Haymitch, Plutarch proposes that Snow keep Haymitch alive to let him see all of his allies and loved ones suffer. Snow likes the plan so much that he proposes the idea of Plutarch becoming a Gamemaker. This scene never happened in the book, but was likely added to the movie to illustrate how well Plutarch is able to play both sides.

In a recent development, silka is the final tribute killed before Haymitch is crowned the victor of the second Quarter Quell, which remains true to the novel. Compared to the movie, the book’s version of events had much more gore. In the novel, Silka has an eyeball dangling from its socket during their battle, and when she successfully swipes at Haymitch’s stomach, his intestines are at risk of falling out.

According to recent reports, in the movie, Katniss and Peeta make an appearance to celebrate Haymitch’s birthday, but this differs slightly from what actually happened. In the novel’s epilogue, Haymitch finally tells the story of his life for the memorial book. The following day, Katniss offers Haymitch goose eggs, while Peeta gives Haymitch an incubator for the eggs to hatch. The movie and book end the same way, with Haymitch sitting in the meadow with his geese, thinking about Lenore Dove.

10 Sophisticated Gourmand Colognes Perfect for Winter

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1007 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Esquire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that if there’s one thing you can trust us on, it’s that we’re always keeping our noses on top of the latest fragrance trends.
  • Instead of buttercream and chocolate sauce, think tonka bean and smoke, bitter cacao and rum, toasted sesame and musk, or vanilla and cardamom.
  • When it comes to gourmands, easily one of the most common base notes is vanilla.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that if there’s one thing you can trust us on, it’s that we’re always keeping our noses on top of the latest fragrance trends. Right now, one is undeniably taking over, just in time for the cold weather: sophisticated gourmands. If “gourmand” brings to mind the sugary cupcake body sprays your sister bought at the mall as a teenager, you’re not alone in that. But these grown-up “neo-gourmands” take the comforting, familiar sweetness of edible notes and balance them with dry woods, spice, or smoke. The result? A little less syrup, a lot more intrigue and sophistication.

Instead of buttercream and chocolate sauce, think tonka bean and smoke, bitter cacao and rum, toasted sesame and musk, or vanilla and cardamom. Even coffee-scented colognes are taking off right now. There are so many delicious upcoming gourmand combinations out there that narrowing them all down to just ten was no easy feat. But we did it, and these are our favorites right now. Consider it your invitation to smell very good (and maybe a little mouthwatering) all winter long.

When it comes to gourmands, easily one of the most common base notes is vanilla. And in fragrance, vanilla definitely does not mean boring—quite the opposite, in fact. Henry Rose’s Dave fragrance combines vanilla and tonka bean at the base for a creamy foundation that’s sweet, but not overwhelmingly sweet.

At the top, we get some nice earthy, slightly spicy notes of tangerine, neroli, and pink pepper, and its heart is softer with florals like orange flower and almond blossom. Base notes of vanilla bean, cocoa, and creamy tonka bean leave you with a smooth, velvety finish.

The great thing about Solférino’s Lumière d’Automne is that it’s both sweet and smoky, but not too much of either. It’s the perfect blend of light gourmand notes (namely vanilla and benzoin) with the hint of smoke that comes from notes of roasted chestnut. The name literally translates to “Autumn Light” and evokes the cozy feeling of wearing a sweater on a chilly day while colorful leaves fall to the ground.

In a recent development, for the past two years, Chai Fleur has been my go-to scent the moment the temperature drops below 50 degrees. I’m not a coffee person, but I do drink a chai latte every day of my life (honestly, I don’t know how I would get through my day without it), and somehow Belnu has captured the scent of chai and turned it into the perfect winter fragrance. It’s sweet and creamy thanks to the base of vanilla and woods, and it has the perfect amount of spice from nutmeg, cinnamon, and green cardamom.

In a recent development, while not technically a gourmand fragrance, Fulton & Roark’s Calle Ocho has notes of bitter chocolate and tonka bean, which give it that velvety smooth feel that many gourmands have, even if it doesn’t smell quite as sweet as a true gourmand. When blended with cinnamon, rum, florals, smoky tobacco leaf, and musk, the chocolate and tonka bean are transformed into something dark, boozy, sexy, and very sophisticated.

Recent findings suggest that sometimes, you don’t have to spend more than $100 to smell like you have your life together. In fact, the whole goal of House of Twist is to make affordable fragrances (under $50!) that smell just like your favorite luxury colognes. Liquid Amber No.173 is a spicy gourmand akin to something like Parfums de Marly’s Althaïr (which we also absolutely love), with spicy cinnamon and cardamom, creamy bourbon vanilla, woods, and musks.

Recent findings suggest that almond is another one of those creamy, nutty scents like pistachio or sesame that thrives in gourmand fragrances. My favorite example of this is Nicolaï Paris’s Macaron Bourbon, an ambery gourmand centered around bitter almond, sweet rum, davana, and patchouli. It’s smooth and creamy without being too rich, so it doesn’t overwhelm you with sweetness. The bitter almond and spices also add an interesting nuttiness to the fragrance, which we love.

Sources indicate that my favorite dessert has got to be a warm sticky toffee pudding with a scoop of vanilla ice cream on top. I never thought there would be a fragrance that captured the warm deliciousness of those exact flavors, but D.S. & Durga, one of our favorite niche fragrance houses, has done just that. Ain’t That Sweet is inspired by a slice of malty date cake and combines notes of cinnamon, date, praline, condensed milk, bourbon vanilla, and nutmeg for an addictive gourmand scent that we’re frankly obsessed with.

In a recent development, you may not expect floral and gourmand notes to go together, but they actually balance each other out quite nicely. In Van Cleef & Arpels’ Orchidée Vanille, the light floral notes of rose and violet lend a nice airiness to the rich gourmand notes of bitter almond, vanilla, and tonka bean. The effect is something sweet but delicate—it’s not the “manliest” of scents in the traditional sense, but we’re very pro-florals when it comes to men’s cologne.

According to recent reports, another one of my favorite fresh gourmands that debuted this year is Abel’s Double Scoop, which truly evokes a sweet, nutty ice cream (my favorite kind). But it’s more nuanced than that—it starts off with herbaceous, slightly woody rosemary before revealing the rich notes of toasted black sesame, butterscotch, and vanilla. The dry down is nice and musky, which gives it a sweet but muted lingering aroma.

It has been revealed that finally, if you do want something rich that still feels grown-up and not too sugary, Free Yourself’s Savor is the way to go. It’s a true gourmand with notes of bittersweet chocolate, pistachio, toasted almond, tonka bean, vanilla, and even marshmallow—but it never feels like an overly sweet, juvenile scent in the way you might think marshmallow would lend itself to. That’s because all these rich, creamy, sweet notes are balanced out by plum, rose, and tobacco, which add a more sophisticated twist to the rich gourmand.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gordon Ramsay has earned 17 Michelin stars throughout his career and still oversees nearly 100 restaurants. He also fronts prime-time TV franchises on both sides of the Atlantic and holds a couple of casual Guinness World Records (call him if you need to fillet a 10-pound fish in 1 minute five seconds).

This is a man who’s never met a goalpost he didn’t want to surpass. So it wasn’t entirely surprising when he posted a bare-chested shot of his six-pack to the grid earlier this month. What generated headlines was the occasion: his 60th birthday. “Gordon Ramsay thirst trap was not on my bingo card,” reads one comment. “My wife is on this app sir,” reads another.

At home in London, he demonstrates me the Insights section on his Instagram account, which reveals the photo has gotten over 62 million impressions. “It’s very strange,” he states. “I’ve had a lot of ribbing from my eldest daughter, Megan. She’s a police officer. She was like, ‘Dad, how can you do that to me?’ All her senior sergeants and officers were laughing and telling her to tell me they’re going for a run. They’re in their early 40s. And then my Royal Marines Commando son just sent me a message with: ‘WTF dad, what are you doing?’”.

It has been revealed that ramsay has been a pretty active guy for a while now, despite working in an industry typically associated with chaotic diets and zero time for exercise. He was a youth soccer player back in the day, before becoming a chef and then, in his 40s, going from weighing 252 pounds to competing in marathons and Ironmans.

All very impressive, but it’s even rarer to be this chiseled in your 60s (maintaining a low body fat percentage becomes harder as your testosterone and growth hormone production slows down). Read on to learn more about his preferred forms of cardio, his favorite pre-workout treat, and why he's established a daily cryotherapy routine. “I call it my freezer,” he says.

According to recent reports, “15 minutes a day. It starts off with a quick two-minute stretch and 100 sit-ups every morning. Precore lifestyle is my ab cruncher thing—these things are fucking amazing, by the way. If I miss a day, then I have to punish it and do double the next day.”.

Industry observers note that “It’s not physically hard with big weights. These are 25 pounds. I’ll do a strength class once a week, 45 minutes. That’s it. Occasional push-ups and squats. No personal trainer.”.

Sources indicate that “What’s helped tremendously, with no impact on any of the joints, is a lot of swimming. So I have an injury in my patella, my right knee, currently. So I just increased the swimming because that’s the only sport that can use every muscle in your body with zero impact. But cardio is off the charts.”.

In a recent development, “I have a Zwift bike, so I jump on that for 45 minutes. There’s no impact on that. I’ll do that Monday, Wednesday, Friday and gear up for 90 minutes on a Sunday. If I wasn’t injured, I’d be doing three 5K runs again, Monday, Wednesday, Friday, 20-minute runs. I’ve got my 5K back down to 21 minutes. The dream is under 20. I was running at 19 and a half back in July. A 5K run is easy to do in the morning before work, it’s done within half an hour. Once I do that, I can gear up for either a two-hour bike on a Sunday or a 90-minute run. I alternate. So, one Sunday’s run, one Sunday’s bike.”.

Recent findings suggest that “10 years ago, I ruptured my Achilles. I invested in an AlterG, a beautiful running machine that takes your weight, so you get all the cardio you want and less impact on the joint.”.

It has been revealed that “From the chef’s perspective, I call it my freezer. It’s the cryochamber. I do two sets of three minutes every morning. I try to go seven days a week in that thing, straight after [working out]. That is incredible. That’ll get up to like minus 160. For six minutes.”.

According to recent reports, “I’ve invested in a tiny little red-light therapy sauna outside in the garden, and it seats two of you, and so [I’ll do] half an hour of that, every other day. This doesn’t need to be done every day. Three times a week’s fine. So when I’m not running, the other day I’ll sit in that red-light therapy and spend 20 minutes, 30 minutes in there, which is brilliant.”.

“The older you get, the more you have to stretch. I use a lot of bands. And so after sitting and stretching, I had those incredible bands where you lift your feet up and pull and stretch. 5 minutes is always a nice stretch before you [work out] and then 10 minutes stretch after that. I’ve never been to a yoga class in my life.”.

According to recent reports, “I’m substantial on oatmeal for breakfast, Monday to Friday. I indulge Saturday, Sunday. I will do [oatmeal with] blueberry compote, caramelized banana for my potassium, and then fresh blueberries on top with some—it sounds weird, but it’s delicious—hot honey.”.

“I have my friends at Precision. I’ll do one of their gels before I start that 5K, a protein gel, 30 grams, and then that sees me through the whole 45-minute routine. Coffee is just a full-fat, flat white, extra hot. Extra hot means I can sip it slowly. I cut out a lot of dairy, a lot of butter, a lot of cream. And so that treat in the morning with a flat white is that sort of, ‘I’ve earned this shit.’”.

“I don’t overstress on that because I stay fit. I monitor what I eat, but if anything, I’ll do smaller portions now. I’ll involve a lot of spinach, involve a lot of salmon, chicken, especially thighs. We’re just smart with less cream, less butter intake. And then when we travel, we just keep it light.”.

It has been revealed that “I have a red wine with dinner, Californian, something light, something delicious. In 20, 30 years running restaurants, I’ve never gone around the room holding a glass of wine, holding a glass of champagne, sitting down, drinking with customers. Again, discipline.”.

Sources indicate that “Just a couple of spoons of creatine, five mornings a week. A little scoop in my water.”.

Industry observers note that “One thing I’ve learned in my 50s and my 60s—everyone said the older you get, the less you sleep. I think it’s the other way around. I like to be in bed by 11, and I’m up at 6. My Oura ring for me has become my best mate, because it just gives me the proper day-by-day indication and then keeps you on track for sleep.”.

It has been revealed that “No, no, no, no, no, no. Definitely not. No. I mean, no. My meditation is Kitchen fucking Nightmares. Dealing with some of those contributors on there and having to sit with them and talk with them. But no, not very good at sitting still.”.
